items.translation: Right is established by nature itself.
items.note: Latin "jus" means both right and law; Vattel renders it "le droit".

items.translation: So that his will stands in place of reason.
items.source: Wolff, Philosophia practica universalis I §132 note
items.note: The phrase adapts Juvenal VI.223, "sit pro ratione voluntas" (let my will stand in place of reason).

items.text: in quo lapsa consuetudo deflexit de via, sensimque eò deducta est, ut honestatem ab utilitate secernens, & constituerit honestum esse aliquod, quod utile non esset, & utile, quod non honestum, quâ nulla pernicies major hominum vita potuit adferri
items.translation: On this point custom slipped and strayed from the path, and was gradually brought to the point where, separating the honourable from the useful, it laid down that something could be honourable that was not useful, and useful that was not honourable: no greater plague than this could have been brought upon human life.
items.note: "vita" is a misprint for "vitæ" (to life), and "& constituerit" stands for Cicero's "constitueret".

items.text: Itaque accepimus, socratem exsecrari solitum eos, qui primùm hæc, naturâ cohærentia opinione distraxissent
items.translation: And so we are told that Socrates used to curse those who first pulled apart in opinion these things that are joined together by nature.

items.text: Atque ipsa utilitas, justi prope mater & æqui
items.translation: And utility itself, almost the mother of the just and the fair.
